fig:latin5.body: The three translations of a Latin square, for one Latin square of order $5$ and one of its transversals. Colours $1,\dots,5$ are red, blue, green, orange and purple. Faint lines show all cells of the square, and thick lines show the cells of the transversal.

conj:euler.heading: Euler, 1782
conj:euler.body: No Latin square of order $n\equiv 2\bmod 4$ decomposes into transversals.

thm:BM.heading: Bowtell and Montgomery [62]
thm:BM.body: A uniformly random Latin square of order $n$ decomposes into transversals with probability $1-o(1)$.

fig:cards.body: A solution of Ozanam's card puzzle (as drawn in [215]). The ranks and the suits form two orthogonal Latin squares of order $4$: every rank–suit pair occurs once. The cards of each suit form a transversal of the square of ranks.

thm:mps-decomp.heading: Montgomery, Pokrovskiy and Sudakov [217]
thm:mps-decomp.body: Every Latin square of order $n$ contains $(1-o(1))n$ disjoint partial transversals, each with $(1-o(1))n$ cells.

thm:room.heading: Mullin and Wallis [222]
thm:room.body: For every $n\geq 4$ there is an optimally coloured $K_{2n}$ which decomposes into rainbow perfect matchings. For $n\in\{2,3\}$ there is none. Equivalently, a Room square of odd side $r$ exists if and only if $r\notin\{3,5\}$.

fig:room.body: A Room square of side $7$ on the symbols $\{0,\dots,6,\infty\}$. Row $i$ is the perfect matching $\{\{\infty,i\}\}\cup\{\{i-j,i+j\}: j=1,2,3\}$ of $K_8$, with indices modulo $7$, and the rows form a $1$-factorisation of $K_8$. Each row has its own colour. Each column is a perfect matching of $K_8$ using one edge from each of four rows, so its four cells have four different colours: it is a rainbow perfect matching for the colouring given by the rows. The seven columns decompose $K_8$.

conj:kotzig.heading: Kotzig, 1963 [183]
conj:kotzig.body: For every $n\geq 2$, the complete graph $K_{2n}$ has a perfect $1$-factorisation.

fig:kotzig.body: Left: in the colouring of $K_8$ by $\mathbb{Z}_2^3$, the colour classes $001$ (red) and $010$ (blue) form two $4$-cycles. Right: the first two rows of the Room square in Figure 3, namely $\{\infty 0,16,25,34\}$ (red) and $\{\infty1,02,36,45\}$ (blue), form a Hamilton cycle. The $1$-factorisation given by the rows of Figure 3 is perfect: any two of its matchings form a Hamilton cycle.

conj:wanless-bipartite.heading: Wanless, 1999 [262]
conj:wanless-bipartite.body: The complete bipartite graph $K_{n,n}$ has a perfect $1$-factorisation if and only if $n=2$ or $n$ is odd.

conj:ryser.heading: Ryser, 1967 [246]
conj:ryser.body: Every Latin square of odd order has a transversal.

fig:blowup.body: Two Latin squares without a transversal. Left: the addition table of $\mathbb{Z}_4$. Right: a Latin square of order $2k$ made of four $k\times k$ Latin squares, where the blue blocks use the symbol set $S_0$ and the orange blocks use $S_1$. A transversal has as many cells in the top-right block as in the bottom-left block, so it has an even number of cells in orange blocks. It also needs all $k$ symbols of $S_1$, which is impossible when $k$ is odd.

thm:hall-paige.heading: Hall and Paige [151]; Wilcox [267], Evans [121] and Bray et al. [66]
thm:hall-paige.body: The multiplication table of a finite group $G$ has a transversal if and only if the Sylow $2$-subgroups of $G$ are trivial or non-cyclic.

fig:queens.body: Five non-attacking queens on the $5\times5$ torus, $\sigma(j)=2j$ on $\mathbb{Z}_5$, shown with a periodic copy to the right; the queens still do not attack each other across the boundary. Here $\sigma(j)+j=3j$ and $\sigma(j)-j=j$ are both bijections of $\mathbb{Z}_5$.

conj:snevily.heading: Snevily, 1999 [252]
conj:snevily.body: Let $G$ be an abelian group of odd order and $A,B\subseteq G$ with $|A|=|B|=k$. Then the $k\times k$ subsquare of the addition table with rows $A$ and columns $B$ has a transversal.

conj:fgt.heading: Friedlander, Gordon and Tannenbaum, 1981 [125]
conj:fgt.body: Let $G$ be an abelian group of order $n$ satisfying the Hall–Paige condition, and let $k\geq 2$ divide $n-1$. Then some orthomorphism of $G$ fixes the identity and permutes the other elements in disjoint cycles of length $k$.

thm:kwan.heading: Kwan [189]
thm:kwan.body: With high probability, a uniformly random Latin square of order $n$ has $((1-o(1))n/e^2)^n$ transversals.

thm:emm.heading: Eberhard, Manners and Mrazović [116]
thm:emm.body: With high probability, a uniformly random Latin square of order $n$ has $(e^{-1/2}+o(1))\, n!^2/n^n$ transversals.

conj:rbs.heading: Ryser–Brualdi–Stein; sources from 1967, 1975, 1991 [246, 70, 253]
conj:rbs.body: Every Latin square of order $n$ has a partial transversal with $n-1$ cells, and a full transversal if $n$ is odd.

thm:kpsy.heading: Keevash, Pokrovskiy, Sudakov and Yepremyan [174]
thm:kpsy.body: Every Latin square of order $n$ has a partial transversal with $n-O(\log n/\log\log n)$ cells.

thm:montgomery-rbs.heading: Montgomery [214]
thm:montgomery-rbs.body: For every sufficiently large $n$, every Latin square of order $n$ has a partial transversal with $n-1$ cells.

conj:multiplicity-rbs.heading: Anastos, Fabian, Müyesser and Szabó, 2022 [34]
conj:multiplicity-rbs.body: Let $K_{n,n}$ be decomposed into perfect matchings $M_1,\dots,M_n$, and let $a_1,\dots,a_n\geq0$ be integers with $a_1+\dots+a_n=n-1$. Then there is a matching $M$ with $|M\cap M_i|=a_i$ for every $i$.

thm:luria.heading: Luria [209]
thm:luria.body: For every $n\equiv 3\bmod 6$, there is a Latin square of order $n$ with at most $((1+o(1))\,2n/(3e^2))^n$ transversals.

conj:akbari-alipour.heading: Akbari and Alipour, 2004 [15]
conj:akbari-alipour.body: For large $n$, every proper colouring of $\Knn$ with at least $n^2/2$ colours has a rainbow perfect matching.

conj:stein.heading: Stein, 1975 [253]
conj:stein.body: Every equi-$n$-square has a partial transversal with $n-1$ cells.

thm:erdos-spencer.heading: Erdős and Spencer [118]
thm:erdos-spencer.body: Every $n\times n$ array in which no symbol appears more than $(n-1)/16$ times has a full transversal.

thm:equi-n.heading: Chakraborti, Christoph, Hunter, Montgomery and Petrov [78]
thm:equi-n.body: Every equi-$n$-square has $n-n^{1-\Omega(1)}$ disjoint partial transversals, each with $n-n^{1-\Omega(1)}$ cells. There are equi-$n$-squares with no partial transversal with more than $n-\Omega(\sqrt n)$ cells.

prob:ps-bounded.heading: Pokrovskiy and Sudakov, 2017 [240]
prob:ps-bounded.body: Does every colouring of $\Knn$ in which each colour appears at most $(1-o(1))n$ times have a rainbow perfect matching?

conj:cchmp.heading: Chakraborti, Christoph, Hunter, Montgomery and Petrov, 2024 [78]
conj:cchmp.body: There is a constant $C$ such that every equi-$n$-square has a partial transversal with at least $n-C\sqrt n$ cells.

conj:stein-one-sided.heading: Stein, 1975 [253]
conj:stein-one-sided.body: Every colouring of $K_{n,n-1}$ in which each vertex of the larger class meets at most one edge of each colour has a rainbow matching with $n-1$ edges.

conj:aharoni-berger.heading: Aharoni and Berger, 2009 [2]
conj:aharoni-berger.body: Any $n$ matchings of size $n+1$ in a bipartite multigraph have a full rainbow matching.

fig:ab-examples.body: Left: three matchings of size $3$ in a bipartite graph with no full rainbow matching, since the only perfect matchings of the $6$-cycle are $M_1$ and $M_2$. In general, $n-1$ copies of $M_1$ and one copy of $M_2$ in a $2n$-cycle show that size $n$ is not enough in Conjecture 2.33. Right: three matchings of size $4$ with no full rainbow matching, since two disjoint edges in a copy of $K_4$ have the same colour. This is why Conjecture 2.37 needs size $n+2$.

thm:drisko.heading: Drisko [112]
thm:drisko.body: Any $2n-1$ matchings of size $n$ in a bipartite graph have a rainbow matching of size $n$.

conj:abchs.heading: Aharoni, Berger, Chudnovsky, Howard and Seymour, 2016 [3]
conj:abchs.body: Any $2n$ matchings of size $n$ in a graph have a rainbow matching of size $n$. If $n$ is odd, $2n-1$ matchings suffice.

conj:grww.heading: Gao, Ramadurai, Wanless and Wormald, 2017 [130]
conj:grww.body: Any $n$ matchings of size $n+2$ in a multigraph have a full rainbow matching.

conj:brouwer.heading: Brouwer, 1981 [67]
conj:brouwer.body: Every Steiner triple system of order $n$ has a matching with at least $(n-4)/3$ edges.

fig:fano.body: The Fano plane, a Steiner triple system of order $7$ whose seven triples are the three sides, the three medians and the circle. Any two triples meet, so its largest matching has one edge, and $1=(7-4)/3$.

conj:ferber-kwan.heading: Ferber and Kwan, 2019 [124]
conj:ferber-kwan.body: Almost every Steiner triple system of order $n\equiv 3\bmod 6$ is resolvable.

thm:suzuki.heading: Suzuki [256]
thm:suzuki.body: An edge-coloured connected graph $G$ on $n$ vertices has a rainbow spanning tree if and only if, for every $1\leq r\leq n-2$, deleting the edges of any $r$ colours leaves a graph with at most $r+1$ components.

thm:abs.heading: Alon, Brualdi and Shader [23]
thm:abs.body: If the edges of $K_n$ are coloured so that every colour class is a complete bipartite graph, then there is a rainbow spanning tree.

fig:graham-pollak.body: Left: $K_4$ partitioned into three complete bipartite graphs, the star at $1$ (red), the star from $2$ to $\{3,4\}$ (blue) and the edge $34$ (green). Right: a rainbow spanning tree. By Theorem 3.2, any partition of $E(K_n)$ into complete bipartite graphs has a rainbow spanning tree, so it has at least $n-1$ parts.

conj:bh.heading: Brualdi and Hollingsworth, 1996 [69]
conj:bh.body: For every $n\geq 3$, every optimal colouring of $K_{2n}$ decomposes into $n$ rainbow spanning trees.

conj:constantine.heading: Constantine, 2002 [92]
conj:constantine.body: For every $n\geq 3$, every optimal colouring of $K_{2n}$ decomposes into $n$ isomorphic rainbow spanning trees.

conj:kks.heading: Kaneko, Kano and Suzuki, 2002 [168]
conj:kks.body: For every $n\geq 6$, every properly coloured $K_n$ contains $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ edge-disjoint rainbow spanning trees.

fig:k4-k6.body: Left: the optimal colouring of $K_4$. Its rainbow spanning trees are the four stars, and any two of them share an edge. Right: three edge-disjoint rainbow spanning trees $T_1,T_2,T_3$ which decompose $K_6$, for the optimal colouring of $K_6$ on $\mathbb{Z}_5\cup\{\infty\}$ in which colour $i$ is $\{\infty i\}\cup\{\{i-j,i+j\}:j=1,2\}$. Colours $0,\dots,4$ are red, blue, green, orange and purple.

thm:mps-trees.heading: Montgomery, Pokrovskiy and Sudakov [217]
thm:mps-trees.body: Every properly coloured $K_n$ contains $(1-o(1))n/2$ edge-disjoint rainbow spanning trees.

thm:gkmo.heading: Glock, Kühn, Montgomery and Osthus [137]
thm:gkmo.body: For every large $n$, every optimal colouring of $K_{2n}$ decomposes into $n$ isomorphic rainbow spanning trees.

thm:xu.heading: Xu [271]
thm:xu.body: For every $\varepsilon>0$ and large $m$, every properly coloured graph with $km$ edges, where $1\leq k\leq 2m$ and every colour class has at most $m$ edges, contains $(1-\varepsilon)m$ edge-disjoint rainbow forests with $k$ edges each. For every $k>2m$ there are such graphs with no rainbow forest with $k$ edges.

thm:mps-embedding.heading: Montgomery, Pokrovskiy and Sudakov [218]
thm:mps-embedding.body: Every locally $k$-bounded colouring of $K_n$ contains a rainbow copy of every tree with at most $(1-o(1))n/k$ vertices.

conj:mps-trees.heading: Montgomery, Pokrovskiy and Sudakov, 2018 [218]
conj:mps-trees.body: There is a constant $C$ such that every properly coloured $K_n$ contains a rainbow copy of every tree on $n-C$ vertices.

conj:graceful.heading: Graceful tree conjecture; Ringel, Kotzig and Rosa, 1960s

conj:ringel.heading: Ringel, 1963
conj:ringel.body: For every tree $T$ with $n$ edges, the complete graph $K_{2n+1}$ decomposes into $2n+1$ copies of $T$.

thm:ringel.heading: Montgomery, Pokrovskiy and Sudakov [219]; Keevash and Staden [175]
thm:ringel.body: Ringel's conjecture holds for all large $n$.

fig:graceful-ringel.body: Left: a graceful labelling of a tree with $4$ edges; edges are coloured by the difference of their labels. Right: $K_7$ on $\mathbb{Z}_7$ with edges coloured by near distance $1$ (red), $2$ (blue) and $3$ (green). The path $0,1,3,6$ is rainbow, and its seven rotations decompose $K_7$, as Ringel's conjecture predicts for the path with $3$ edges.

thm:harmonious.heading: Müyesser and Pokrovskiy [225]
thm:harmonious.body: For every $\Delta$ there is $n_0$ such that, for $n\geq n_0$, the coloured complete graph $K_{\mathbb{Z}_n}$ contains a rainbow copy of every tree on $n$ vertices with maximum degree at most $\Delta$.

conj:rota.heading: Rota, 1989; see Huang and Rota [160]
conj:rota.body: Let $B_1,\dots,B_n$ be bases of an $n$-dimensional vector space. Then the $n^2$ vectors can be split into $n$ disjoint bases, each containing exactly one vector from each $B_i$.

fig:rota.body: Left: Rota's conjecture for three bases of $\mathbb{R}^3$, with vectors written as coordinate strings. The rows are the given bases $B_1,B_2,B_3$, and each column has determinant $1$, so each column is a basis; $6$ of the $36$ ways to order rows $2$ and $3$ work. Right: the graphic case with $n=2$. The edges of a red and a blue spanning tree of a multigraph on $\{a,b,c\}$ split into the rainbow spanning trees $\{ab_{\mathrm{red}},ac\}$ and $\{bc,ab_{\mathrm{blue}}\}$.

conj:alon-tarsi.heading: Alon and Tarsi, 1992 [31]
conj:alon-tarsi.body: For every even $n$, the numbers of even and odd Latin squares of order $n$ are different.

thm:montgomery-sauermann.heading: Montgomery and Sauermann [220]
thm:montgomery-sauermann.body: Let $B_1,\dots,B_n$ be bases of a matroid of rank $n$. Then there are $(1-o(1))n$ disjoint bases, each containing exactly one element of each $B_i$. Moreover, the $n^2$ elements can be covered by $(1+o(1))n$ such bases.

conj:kahn.heading: Kahn, 1994 [160]
conj:kahn.body: Let $B_{i,j}$, $1\leq i,j\leq n$, be bases of a matroid of rank $n$. Then there are elements $b_{i,j}\in B_{i,j}$ such that every row $\{b_{i,1},\dots,b_{i,n}\}$ and every column $\{b_{1,j},\dots,b_{n,j}\}$ is a basis.

conj:matroid-rbs.heading: Aharoni and Berger, 2009 [2]
conj:matroid-rbs.body: Let $M$ and $N$ be matroids on the same ground set, and let $F_1,\dots,F_n$ be disjoint sets of size $n$, each independent in both $M$ and $N$. Then there is a set of size $n-1$, independent in both $M$ and $N$, containing at most one element of each $F_i$.

fig:collection.body: Left: a collection of three graphs on four vertices. Right: the same collection as an edge-coloured multigraph, in which $G_i$ supplies the edges of colour $i$. The thick edges form a Hamilton path $1\,4\,3\,2$ with one edge from each graph, that is, a transversal.

thm:mmp-trees.heading: Montgomery, Müyesser and Pehova [216]
thm:mmp-trees.body: For each $\alpha>0$ there are $c>0$ and $n_0$ such that the following holds for all $n\geq n_0$. If each of $n-1$ graphs on a common set of $n$ vertices has minimum degree at least $(1/2+\alpha)n$, then the collection contains a transversal copy of every $n$-vertex tree with maximum degree at most $cn/\log n$.

thm:frieze-mckay.heading: Frieze and McKay [126]
thm:frieze-mckay.body: In the randomly coloured random graph process with at least $n-1$ colours, with high probability the first graph that contains a rainbow spanning tree is the first graph that is connected and uses at least $n-1$ colours.

thm:kls-trees.heading: Katsamaktsis, Letzter and Sgueglia [171]
thm:kls-trees.body: For every $\delta\in(0,1)$ and integer $d\geq2$ there is $C>0$ such that the following holds. Let $T$ be an $n$-vertex tree with maximum degree at most $d$, and let $G_0$ be an $n$-vertex graph with $\delta(G_0)\geq\delta n$. If $G_0\cup G(n,C/n)$ is coloured uniformly with $n-1$ colours, then with high probability it contains a rainbow copy of $T$.

fig:maamoun-meyniel.body: The colouring of $K_4$ by $\mathbb{Z}_2^2$, where $xy$ has colour $x+y$. A Hamilton path has three edges, so a rainbow one would use each colour once, and the sum of its colours would be $01+10+11=00$. But this sum equals the sum of the two endpoints, which are distinct. Hence there is no rainbow Hamilton path. The same holds for $K_{2^k}$ for every $k\geq 2$.

conj:andersen.heading: Andersen, 1989 [36]
conj:andersen.body: Every properly coloured $K_n$ contains a rainbow path with $n-1$ vertices.

thm:andersen.heading: Bowtell, Montgomery, Müyesser and Pokrovskiy [63]
thm:andersen.body: For every sufficiently large $n$, every properly coloured $K_n$ contains a rainbow path with $n-1$ vertices.

prob:aemm.heading: Akbari, Etesami, Mahini and Mahmoody, 2007 [17]
prob:aemm.body: Does every $1$-factorisation of $K_n$ contain a rainbow cycle through all but two vertices?

thm:schrijver.heading: Bucić, Frederickson, Müyesser, Pokrovskiy and Yepremyan [71]
thm:schrijver.body: Every properly coloured $d$-regular graph contains a rainbow path with $(1-o(1))d$ edges.

conj:chen-li.heading: Chen and Li, 2005 [83]
conj:chen-li.body: Every edge-coloured graph in which every vertex is incident with edges of at least $d$ colours contains a rainbow path with $d-1$ edges.

fig:walecki.body: Walecki's decomposition of $K_7$ into three Hamilton cycles, $\infty,0,1,5,2,4,3$ and its two rotations. Each cycle is one round of the dance for seven children.

conj:graham.heading: Graham, 1971 [144]
conj:graham.body: Let $p$ be a prime and $S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_p\setminus\{0\}$. Then the elements of $S$ can be ordered as $s_1,\dots,s_k$ so that the partial sums $s_1,\,s_1+s_2,\,\dots,\,s_1+\dots+s_k$ are distinct.

fig:graham.body: The Cayley digraph of $\mathbb{Z}_7$ with $S=\{1,3,4\}$, edges coloured by the generator. The ordering $3,4,1$ has partial sums $3,0,1$, which are distinct, and gives the rainbow path $3\to0\to1$ (bold) with colours $4$ and $1$. The ordering $1,3,4$ has partial sums $1,4,1$ and fails. Four of the six orderings work.

thm:graham.heading: Pham and Sauermann [234], with [48, 47]
thm:graham.body: Graham's rearrangement conjecture holds for all sufficiently large primes $p$.

thm:kuang-wang.heading: Kuang and Wang [187]
thm:kuang-wang.body: There is an absolute constant $n_0$ such that, for every finite abelian group $G$, every set $S\subseteq G\setminus\{0\}$ with $|S|\geq n_0$ has an ordering with distinct partial sums.

prob:directed-schrijver.heading: Directed Schrijver problem; Bucić, Frederickson, Müyesser, Pokrovskiy and Yepremyan, 2025 [71]
prob:directed-schrijver.body: Let $D$ be a $d$-regular digraph, in which every vertex has indegree and outdegree $d$, whose edges are coloured with $d$ colours so that each vertex has one incoming and one outgoing edge of each colour. Does $D$ contain a rainbow directed path with $d-1$ edges?

thm:wilson.heading: Wilson [269]
thm:wilson.body: Every $d$-regular digraph, properly coloured with $d$ colours as in Problem 4.9, contains a rainbow directed path with $d-o(d)$ edges.

prob:all-groups.heading: Bedert, Bucić, Kravitz, Montgomery and Müyesser, 2025 [47]
prob:all-groups.body: Does every subset of every finite group, not containing the identity, have an ordering with distinct partial products?

conj:ch.heading: Caccetta and Häggkvist, 1978
conj:ch.body: Every digraph on $n$ vertices with minimum outdegree at least $r$ contains a directed cycle of length at most $\lceil n/r\rceil$.

conj:aharoni-cycle.heading: Aharoni, 2017
conj:aharoni-cycle.body: Let $G$ be a simple graph on $n$ vertices whose edges are coloured with $n$ colours, each used at least $r$ times. Then $G$ contains a rainbow cycle of length at most $\lceil n/r\rceil$.

fig:tail-colouring.body: The reduction from the Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture to Aharoni's conjecture. Each edge $u\to v$ becomes an undirected edge of colour $u$ (vertex $1$ red, $2$ blue, $3$ green, $4$ orange). The rainbow triangle $1,2,3$ comes from the directed triangle $1\to2\to3\to1$.

fig:hypercube.body: The cube $Q_3$ with each edge coloured by the coordinate in which its endpoints differ. This colouring is proper, and every cycle uses each colour an even number of times, so no cycle is rainbow.

fig:kikuchi.body: An edge of the Kikuchi graph with $k=4$ and $\ell=4$. A filled dot in a row means that the vertex belongs to that set. The sets $S=\{1,2,5,6\}$ and $T=\{3,4,5,6\}$ differ on $E=\{1,2,3,4\}$. If $E$ is an edge of $H$, the corresponding Kikuchi vertices are joined by an edge of colour $E$.

thm:ldc-cubic.heading: Alrabiah, Guruswami, Kothari and Manohar [33]
thm:ldc-cubic.body: For fixed positive error tolerance and decoding advantage, every binary $3$-query locally decodable code with $m$ message bits has length $n=\widetilde{\Omega}(m^3)$.

conj:kmsv.heading: Keevash, Mubayi, Sudakov and Verstraëte, 2007 [173]
conj:kmsv.body: There is a constant $C$ such that every properly coloured graph on $n$ vertices with at least $Cn\log n$ edges contains a rainbow cycle.

thm:rainbow-dirac.heading: Coulson and Perarnau [100]
thm:rainbow-dirac.body: There is $\mu>0$ such that, for large $n$, every graph on $n$ vertices with minimum degree at least $n/2$ contains a rainbow Hamilton cycle in every colouring in which each colour is used at most $\mu n$ times.

conj:peng-yan.heading: Peng and Yan, 2024 [233]
conj:peng-yan.body: Every proper colouring of a graph on $n$ vertices with minimum degree at least $n/2$, in which each colour is used at most $n/8$ times, contains a rainbow Hamilton cycle.

fig:factor-colours.body: Two triangle-factors. Left: each triangle is rainbow, but the colours recur in the other component. Right: all six colours are distinct. Edge labels identify the colours.

thm:yuster-factors.heading: Yuster [273]
thm:yuster-factors.body: For every fixed graph $F$ with at least one edge there is a constant $C=C(F)$ with the following property. If $v(F)$ divides $n$ and $G$ is an $n$-vertex graph with \[ \delta(G)\geq \left(1-\frac{1}{\chi(F)}\right)n+C, \] then every proper edge-colouring of $G$ contains a spanning tiling by rainbow copies of $F$.

conj:muyesser-triangles.heading: Müyesser, 2023 [223]
conj:muyesser-triangles.body: There is an absolute constant $C$ such that every complete graph $K_n$ properly coloured with $n$ colours contains a rainbow union of vertex-disjoint triangles covering all but at most $C$ vertices.

thm:egj-spanning.heading: Ehard, Glock and Joos [117]
thm:egj-spanning.body: For all $d\in(0,1]$, $\gamma\in(0,1)$ and integers $\Delta,\Lambda\geq1$, there are $\varepsilon>0$ and $n_0$ such that the following holds for $n\geq n_0$. Let $G$ be an $(\varepsilon,d)$-quasirandom graph on $n$ vertices and let $H$ have $n$ vertices, at least one edge and maximum degree at most $\Delta$. Every locally $\Lambda$-bounded, globally $(1-\gamma)e(G)/e(H)$-bounded colouring of $G$ contains a rainbow copy of $H$.

conj:egj-cyclic.heading: Ehard, Glock and Joos, 2019 [117]
conj:egj-cyclic.body: For every integer $\Delta\geq1$ there is $n_0$ such that, for all $n\geq n_0$, every graph $H$ with $n$ edges and maximum degree at most $\Delta$ has a cyclic decomposition of $K_{2n+1}$ into copies of $H$.

fig:cyclic.body: (a) In $K_7$ on $\mathbb{Z}_7$, the triangle $0,1,3$ is rainbow in the near-distance colouring; its edges have near distances $1$, $2$ and $3$. (b) Its seven rotations $\{i,i+1,i+3\}$, one colour each, partition the $21$ edges of $K_7$; the copies form the Fano plane. A computer check confirms the partition.

fig:golomb.body: The marks $0,1,4,6$ form a Golomb ruler. Left: the six distances, coloured and labelled by length. Right: the same six distances colour the edges of a rainbow $K_4$; vertex labels are the marks.

thm:bkp-spanning.heading: Böttcher, Kohayakawa and Procacci [59]
thm:bkp-spanning.body: Let $H$ have $n$ vertices and maximum degree at most $\Delta$, where $\Delta\geq1$. Every globally $n/(51\Delta^2)$-bounded colouring of $K_n$ contains a rainbow copy of $H$.

thm:sv-cherries.heading: Sudakov and Volec [255]
thm:sv-cherries.body: If $H$ is an $n$-vertex graph with at most $r$ cherries, then every globally $n/(1512\,r^{3/4})$-bounded colouring of $K_n$ contains a rainbow copy of $H$.

thm:ckpy-graph-factors.heading: Coulson, Keevash, Perarnau and Yepremyan [99]
thm:ckpy-graph-factors.body: For every fixed graph $F$ with at least one edge and every $\varepsilon>0$, there are $\mu>0$ and $n_0$ such that the following holds. If $n\geq n_0$, $v(F)\mid n$ and $\delta(G)\geq(\delta_F+\varepsilon)n$, then every globally $\mu n$-bounded colouring of $G$ contains a rainbow $F$-factor.

thm:rainbow-bandwidth.heading: Glock and Joos [136]
thm:rainbow-bandwidth.body: For all $\varepsilon>0$ and integers $\Delta\geq1$, $r\geq2$, there are $\beta,\mu>0$ and $n_0$ such that the following holds for $n\geq n_0$. Let $H$ be an $r$-colourable graph on $n$ vertices with maximum degree at most $\Delta$ and bandwidth at most $\beta n$. If $G$ has $n$ vertices and minimum degree at least $(1-1/r+\varepsilon)n$, then every globally $\mu n$-bounded colouring of $G$ contains a rainbow copy of $H$.

fig:mmp.body: The obstruction of Montgomery, Müyesser and Pehova for $F=C_4$ and $n=8$. The eight graphs consist of seven copies of the graph in (a) and the graph in (b). In (c), a $4$-cycle meeting both $A$ and $B$ uses two edges between them, and both must come from $G_8$. A computer check confirms that none of the $315$ $C_4$-factors of $K_8$ is a transversal.

thm:mmp-factors.heading: Montgomery, Müyesser and Pehova [216]
thm:mmp-factors.body: Let $\varepsilon>0$ and let $F$ be a graph with $r$ vertices and $t$ edges. For all sufficiently large $n$, every collection of $tn$ graphs on a common set of $rn$ vertices, each with minimum degree at least $(\delta_F^{\mathrm T}+\varepsilon)rn$, contains a transversal $F$-factor.

thm:ghmps-powers.heading: Gupta, Hamann, Müyesser, Parczyk and Sgueglia [149]
thm:ghmps-powers.body: Let $r\geq2$ and $\varepsilon>0$. For all sufficiently large $n$, every collection of $rn$ graphs on a common set of $n$ vertices, each with minimum degree at least $(r/(r+1)+\varepsilon)n$, contains a transversal $r$-th power of a Hamilton cycle.

fig:lw-obstruction.body: The Lo–Williams construction for $t=1$. Left: the vertex sets and complete pairs; $Y\cup Z$ induces a clique. The edges in $G[X]$ and $G[Y\cup Z]$ all have distinct colours. Right: edges from $X$ to a fixed $y$ have colour $c_y$, excluding triangles with two vertices in $X$. A rainbow triangle through $X$ needs two vertices of $Y$, but $|Y|=11<2|X|$.

thm:lw-tiling.heading: Lo and Williams [201]
thm:lw-tiling.body: For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $n_0$ such that every edge-coloured graph $G$ on $n\geq n_0$ vertices with $3\mid n$ and \[ \delta^c(G)\geq(5/6+\varepsilon)n \] has a spanning tiling by rainbow triangles.

conj:lw-clique-tiling.heading: Lo and Williams, 2024 [201]
conj:lw-clique-tiling.body: For every integer $r\geq3$ and all sufficiently large $n$ divisible by $r$, every edge-coloured graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with \[ \delta^c(G)\geq\left(1-\frac{r-1}{r^2-2}\right)n \] contains a spanning tiling by rainbow copies of $K_r$.

thm:kkko-factors.heading: Kim, Kühn, Kupavskii and Osthus [178]
thm:kkko-factors.body: Fix a graph $F$ with $f$ vertices and $h\geq1$ edges, and let $0<\alpha<1$. There are $\eta>0$ and $n_0$ such that, whenever $n\geq n_0$ and $f\mid n$, every colouring of $K_n$ which is globally $(1-\alpha)fn/(2h)$-bounded and locally $\eta n/\log^{2a(F)}n$-bounded has an $\alpha$-decomposition into rainbow $F$-factors.

thm:han-yuan.heading: Han and Yuan [152]
thm:han-yuan.body: There is a constant $K$ such that, for every finite $X$, increasing family $\mathcal F\subseteq 2^X$ and integer $k\geq\ell$, the $k$-colour rainbow threshold of $\mathcal F$ is at most $K\,q_f(\mathcal F)\log\ell$, where $q_f(\mathcal F)$ is the fractional expectation threshold.

thm:bmmp-directed.heading: Bowtell, Montgomery, Müyesser and Pokrovskiy [63]
thm:bmmp-directed.body: There is $n_0$ such that, for $n\geq n_0$, every proper colouring of the complete digraph with loops on $n$ vertices using $n$ colours contains a rainbow path on $n-1$ vertices.

thm:bps-directed.heading: Benzing, Pokrovskiy and Sudakov [51]
thm:bps-directed.body: Every properly coloured complete digraph on $n$ vertices contains a rainbow cycle of length $n-O(n^{4/5})$, and a rainbow union of vertex-disjoint paths with $n-O(n^{2/3})$ edges.

conj:gould-kelly.heading: Gould and Kelly, 2021 [142]
conj:gould-kelly.body: Every proper colouring of the complete digraph with loops on $n$ vertices contains a rainbow path or a rainbow cycle with at least $n-1$ edges.

fig:colour-degree.body: Left: an edge-coloured graph. Right: at each vertex one edge of each colour is chosen and oriented away from the vertex; the arrows keep the colour of their edge. The outdegree of every vertex equals its colour degree. The edges $bd$ and $db$, for example, are chosen at $b$ and at $d$ respectively.

thm:cmno.heading: Czygrinow, Molla, Nagle and Oursler [102]
thm:cmno.body: Let $\ell\geq4$ be fixed and let $n$ be sufficiently large. If $\ell$ is even, every edge-coloured graph on $n$ vertices with minimum colour degree at least $(n+5)/3$ contains a rainbow cycle of length $\ell$. For every $\ell$, every oriented graph on $n$ vertices with minimum outdegree at least $(n+1)/3$ contains a cycle of length $\ell$.

fig:efx.body: A $2$-partite digraph in which every vertex has an inneighbour in the other part. Each edge is coloured by the part containing its final vertex. The only cycle, $a_1b_1a_2b_2a_1$, uses two vertices from each part and two edges of each colour, so it is not rainbow. Hence $R(2)\geq2$.

thm:sivashankar.heading: Sivashankar [251]
thm:sivashankar.body: For every positive integer $d$, we have $R(d)<ed$.

prob:rainbow-cycle-number.heading: Berendsohn, Boyadzhiyska and Kozma, 2022 [52]
prob:rainbow-cycle-number.body: Is $R(d)=d$ for every positive integer $d$?

fig:zero-sum.body: (a) A labelling of the complete digraph on two vertices by $\mathbb{Z}_2$; its only cycle has label sum $1$. (b) The lift: $(i,x)$ is joined to $(j,x+a_{ij})$, and edges are coloured by the part of the final vertex. The lift is the digraph of Figure 26; its only cycle is not rainbow. A computer check confirms both statements.

conj:arborescence.heading: Rainbow arborescence conjecture; Bérczi, Király, Yamaguchi and Yokoi, 2024 [74]
conj:arborescence.body: If the edges of a digraph on $n$ vertices are coloured with $n-1$ colours so that each colour class is a spanning arborescence, then there is a spanning arborescence with exactly one edge of each colour.

fig:arborescence.body: Left: three spanning arborescences on four vertices, rooted at $1$ (red path), $4$ (blue star) and $2$ (green). Right: a rainbow arborescence rooted at $4$, with one edge of each colour. This example has six rainbow arborescences in total.

fig:tournaments.body: Two tournaments on $\{1,2,3\}$. A transversal Hamilton path would consist of an edge of $T_1$ followed by an edge of $T_2$, or the other way round. A computer check of all six orderings confirms that none exists.

thm:ckls.heading: Chakraborti, Kim, Lee and Seo [79]
thm:ckls.body: For every sufficiently large $n$, every collection of $n-1$ tournaments on a common set of $n$ vertices contains a transversal Hamilton path. Every collection of $n$ tournaments on $n$ vertices, all but at most one of which are strongly connected, contains a transversal Hamilton cycle.

thm:clsw.heading: Cheng, Li, Sun and Wang [86]
thm:clsw.body: For every sufficiently large $n$, every collection of $n$ digraphs on a common set of $n$ vertices, each with minimum semidegree at least $n/2$, contains a transversal Hamilton cycle.

conj:ckls-connected.heading: Chakraborti, Kim, Lee and Seo, 2023 [79]
conj:ckls-connected.body: For all sufficiently large $n$, every strongly rainbow-connected collection of $n$ tournaments on a common set of $n$ vertices contains a transversal Hamilton cycle.

prob:oriented-transversal.heading: Cheng, Li, Sun and Wang, 2025 [86]
prob:oriented-transversal.body: Let $D_1,\dots,D_n$ be oriented graphs on a common set of $n$ vertices, each with minimum semidegree at least $\lceil(3n-4)/8\rceil$. Must the collection contain a transversal Hamilton cycle?

thm:krueger-staudinger.heading: Krueger and Staudinger [186]
thm:krueger-staudinger.body: For every $\alpha>0$ there is $C>0$ such that the following holds. Let $D_0$ be a digraph on $n$ vertices with $\delta^0(D_0)\geq\alpha n$. If $D_0\cup D(n,C/n)$ is coloured uniformly from $[n]$, then with high probability it contains a rainbow copy of every orientation of every cycle of length between $2$ and $n$, simultaneously.

fig:colour-vertices.body: Left: a coloured $4$-cycle. Right: each edge receives a new vertex for its colour (squares), giving a $3$-graph. The edges $ab$ and $da$ have the same colour, so their triples share the vertex $c_1$. A computer check of all sets of edges confirms that rainbow matchings on the left are exactly matchings on the right.

fig:egz.body: Alon's construction for $r=t=3$. Left: the four points of $\mathbb{Z}_3^2$ shown in black, each taken twice, form a sequence of length $8$ in which no three terms sum to zero. Right: the vector $(1,0)$ gives the perfect matching with edges $(1,0,0)$, $(2,1,1)$, $(0,2,2)$. A computer check confirms that the eight matchings have no rainbow matching of size $3$.

thm:psz.heading: Pohoata, Sauermann and Zakharov [235]
thm:psz.body: For every fixed $r\geq3$ there are $c_r,C_r>0$ such that the following holds for every $t\geq2$. Some family of $c_rt^r$ matchings of size $t$ in an $r$-partite $r$-graph has no rainbow matching of size $t$, while any $C_rt^r$ matchings of size $t$ in any $r$-graph have a rainbow matching of size $t$.

thm:bfky.heading: Bowtell, Freschi, Kronenberg and Yan [60]
thm:bfky.body: For every fixed $r\geq3$ and sufficiently large $n$, \[ \frac{2n}{r+1}-O_r(1)\leq g'(r,n)\leq g(r,n)\leq n-\Omega_r\bigl(n^{1-1/r}\bigr). \]

conj:near-full.heading: Bowtell, Freschi, Kronenberg and Yan, 2025 [60]
conj:near-full.body: For every fixed $r\geq2$, each of $g(r,n)$, $g'(r,n)$, $h(r,n)$ and $h'(r,n)$ is $(1+o(1))n$.

fig:list-colouring.body: Left: a path $abcd$ in which every edge has the list $\{1,2\}$. Right: each edge $e$ and colour $a\in L(e)$ give a copy of $e$ in layer $a$, coloured by $e$. A full rainbow matching takes one copy of each edge, and the copies must be disjoint. The thick copies give the colouring $1,2,1$. A computer check confirms that the full rainbow matchings correspond exactly to the two proper colourings $1,2,1$ and $2,1,2$.

conj:rainbow-emc.heading: Huang, Loh and Sudakov, 2012 [159]; Aharoni and Howard, 2016 [10]
conj:rainbow-emc.body: Let $n\geq km$. If $\mathcal F_1,\dots,\mathcal F_m$ are families of $k$-element subsets of $[n]$, each with more than $f(n,m,k)$ members, then there are pairwise disjoint sets $F_1\in\mathcal F_1,\dots,F_m\in\mathcal F_m$.

fig:mms.body: Two agents and four items $e_{11},e_{12},e_{21},e_{22}$. Agent $1$ accepts a bundle only if it contains a row, and agent $2$ only if it contains a column. Every row meets every column, so the two perfect matchings have no rainbow matching of size $2$, and there is no MMS allocation.

thm:feige.heading: Feige [122]
thm:feige.body: Let $\mu(n)$ be the largest $m$ such that every instance with $n$ agents with monotone valuations and at most $m$ goods has an MMS allocation. Then $\mu(n)=n+\Theta(\log n)$.

thm:you.heading: You [272]
thm:you.body: Let $k\geq3$ and $k/2\leq\ell\leq k-1$. For sufficiently large $n$ divisible by $k$, if $H_1,\dots,H_{n/k}$ are $k$-graphs on a common set of $n$ vertices with $\delta_\ell(H_i)>\delta(n,k,\ell)$ for every $i$, then they have a rainbow perfect matching.

conj:twwy.heading: Tang, Wang, Wang and Yan, 2023 [258]
conj:twwy.body: For all $1\leq d\leq k-1$ and $\mu>0$ there is $n_0$ such that, for $n\geq n_0$, every collection of $n$ $k$-graphs on a common set of $n$ vertices, each with minimum $d$-degree at least $h_d(k,n)+\mu n^{k-d}$, has a rainbow tight Hamilton cycle.

thm:ckpy-hyper.heading: Coulson, Keevash, Perarnau and Yepremyan [99]
thm:ckpy-hyper.body: Let $1\leq\ell<k$, let $F$ be a $k$-graph on $h$ vertices, and let $\varepsilon>0$. There is $\mu>0$ such that for large $n$ divisible by $h$, every $k$-graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with $\delta_\ell(G)\geq(\delta^*_\ell(F)+\varepsilon)n^{k-\ell}$ has a rainbow $F$-factor in every $\mu$-bounded colouring. Here $\delta^*_\ell(F)$ is the asymptotic $\ell$-degree threshold for an $F$-factor.

thm:kmp.heading: Kathapurkar, Morris and Perarnau [169]
thm:kmp.body: Let $1\leq j<k$ and $\varepsilon>0$. There is $\mu>0$ such that for large $n$ divisible by $k-1$ the following holds. If $G$ is an $n$-vertex $k$-graph with $\delta_j(G)$ at least $\varepsilon n^{k-j}$ above the $j$-degree threshold for a loose Hamilton cycle, then every colouring of $G$ with at most $\mu n^{k-1}$ edges of each colour has a rainbow loose Hamilton cycle.

fig:tight-obstruction.body: The construction of Kathapurkar, Morris and Perarnau. Triples with two vertices in one part are edges, coloured by that pair. Where a tight cycle first reaches $V_3$, the two previous vertices lie in one part, so two consecutive triples have the same colour. A computer check for $n=6$ finds eight tight Hamilton cycles, none of them rainbow.

fig:latin-cube.body: The Latin cube of order $3$ with entries $i+j+k\bmod 3$, shown layer by layer. The shaded entries $(0,0,0)$, $(1,1,2)$ and $(2,2,1)$ have symbols $0,1,2$ and no common coordinate, so they form a transversal.

conj:latin-hypercube.heading: Wanless, 2011 [264]
conj:latin-hypercube.body: If $n$ or $d$ is odd, then every Latin hypercube of dimension $d$ and order $n$ has a transversal.

stmt-2.6.heading: Glock and Sgueglia [138]
stmt-2.6.body: For every $k$ there is $C$ such that, if $p\geq C\log n/n$, then with high probability the random graph $G(2n,p)$ contains $k$ edge-disjoint perfect matchings, any two of which form a Hamilton cycle.

stmt-2.7.heading: Cheng and Sgueglia [87]
stmt-2.7.body: The complete graph $K_{2n}$ has a $1$-factorisation in which $(1-o(1))2n$ of the perfect matchings have the property that any two of them form a Hamilton cycle.

stmt-2.10.heading: Mann [212]; Paige [232]
stmt-2.10.body: The multiplication table of a finite group $G$ has an orthogonal mate if and only if $G$ has a complete mapping.

stmt-2.12.heading: Eberhard, Manners and Mrazović [114]
stmt-2.12.body: For odd $n$, the addition table of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ has $(e^{-1/2}+o(1))\,n\,n!^2/n^n$ transversals.

stmt-2.15.heading: Müyesser [223]
stmt-2.15.body: The Friedlander–Gordon–Tannenbaum conjecture holds for all sufficiently large groups.

stmt-2.17.heading: Gould and Kelly [142]
stmt-2.17.body: With high probability, a uniformly random Latin square has a Hamilton transversal.

stmt-2.25.heading: Keevash and Yepremyan [177]; Montgomery, Pokrovskiy and Sudakov [217]
stmt-2.25.body: There is $\varepsilon>0$ such that, for large $n$, every proper colouring of $\Knn$ with at least $n^{2-\varepsilon}$ colours has a rainbow perfect matching. In particular, Conjecture 2.24 holds.

stmt-2.28.heading: Pokrovskiy and Sudakov [240]
stmt-2.28.body: For large $n$, there are equi-$n$-squares with no partial transversal with more than $n-\frac{1}{42}\ln n$ cells.

stmt-2.34.heading: Pokrovskiy [237]
stmt-2.34.body: Any $n$ matchings of size $n+o(n)$ in a bipartite multigraph have a full rainbow matching.

stmt-2.38.heading: Correia, Pokrovskiy and Sudakov [94]
stmt-2.38.body: For large $n$, any $n$ matchings of size at least $n+20n^{1-1/16}$ in a multigraph have a full rainbow matching.

stmt-2.39.heading: Correia and Sudakov [95]
stmt-2.39.body: For large $n$, $v(n)=3n-2$. This proves a conjecture of Grinblat.

stmt-2.40.heading: Kostochka and Yancey [181]
stmt-2.40.body: Every edge-coloured graph $G$ has a rainbow matching of size $\lceil\delta^c(G)/2\rceil$.

stmt-2.42.heading: Montgomery [214]
stmt-2.42.body: For large $n$, every Steiner triple system of order $n$ has a matching with $\lfloor n/3\rfloor-1$ edges. In particular, Conjecture 2.41 holds for large $n$.

stmt-3.11.heading: Crawford, Sankar, Schildkraut and Spiro [101]
stmt-3.11.body: Every proper colouring of the hypercube $Q_n$ contains a rainbow copy of every tree with at most $n$ edges.

stmt-4.15.heading: Alon, Bucić, Sauermann, Zakharov and Zamir [24]
stmt-4.15.body: Every properly coloured graph on $n$ vertices with average degree at least $(\log n)^{1+o(1)}$ contains a rainbow cycle.
